title: Numbers, and what things cost
goal: Count to a million, understand a price said at speed, and handle the everyday arithmetic of Indonesian life — where a bowl of noodles costs fifteen thousand and nobody blinks.
bekal: count from nol to seratus and build any number up to sejuta
ask and understand *Berapa harganya?* and the answer
recognise *ribu*, *rebu* and the shortcut where the thousands are simply dropped

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di pasar
dialogs.intro: A traditional market on a Saturday morning. Sarah wants mangoes; Pak Joko sells fruit.

lines.speaker: Joko:
lines.text: Dua puluh lima ribu sekilo, Mbak.
lines.literal: two ten five thousand one-kilo, miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dua puluh lima ribu? Mahal, Pak.
lines.literal: two ten five thousand? expensive, Mr.

lines.speaker: Joko:
lines.text: Ini manis sekali, Mbak. Coba dulu.
lines.id: They're very sweet. Try one first.
lines.literal: this sweet very, miss. try first.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Can you come down? Twenty thousand?

lines.speaker: Joko:
lines.text: Dua puluh dua, deh. Untuk Mbak saja.
lines.literal: two ten two, then. for miss only.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: All right. I'll take two kilos.

lines.speaker: Joko:
lines.text: Dua kilo, empat puluh empat ribu.
lines.literal: two kilo, four ten four thousand.

lines.speaker: Joko:
lines.text: Kembaliannya enam ribu. Terima kasih, Mbak.
lines.id: Six thousand change. Thank you, miss.
lines.literal: change-its six thousand. thank you, miss.

notes: **Prices in Indonesia are large numbers, and this is the real listening challenge.** A cheap meal is *lima belas ribu* (15,000), a taxi ride *lima puluh ribu* (50,000), a month's rent might be *tiga juta* (3,000,000). Your ear has to get comfortable with *ribu* and *juta* fast, because everything you buy will be counted in them.
**Berapa on its own is a complete question.** *Mangga ini berapa?* — "these mangoes, how much?" You do not need *harganya*, though *Berapa harganya?* is equally correct and slightly more polite.

**Boleh kurang? is the polite way to open a bargain.** Literally "may (it be) less?". In a traditional market this is expected, cheerful and part of the transaction. In a supermarket, a chain café or anywhere with a printed price tag, it is not — the price is the price.
**Deh** in *Dua puluh dua, deh* is another of those toneless particles: it marks a concession, roughly "all right then". It is the sound of a seller giving in with good humour.

**Kembalian means change**, from *kembali* ("to return"). If the seller has none, you will hear *Ada uang pas?* — "do you have the exact money?" Carrying small notes is a genuine survival skill in Indonesia.

grammars.title: 0 to 100 — three rules and you are done
body: Learn one to ten, then watch what happens to them.
after: **Rule 1 — the teens take *belas*.** Eleven to nineteen are simply the digit plus *belas*: *dua belas*, *tiga belas*, *tujuh belas*. The only irregular one is eleven, *sebelas*.
**Rule 2 — the tens take *puluh*.** *Dua puluh* is literally "two tens". Then you just add: *dua puluh tiga* = 23.

**Rule 3 — *se-* means "one".** Instead of *satu puluh*, *satu ratus*, *satu ribu*, Indonesian glues *se-* on: *sepuluh*, *seratus*, *seribu*, *sejuta*. You will meet this *se-* again in *sekilo* (one kilo) and *sehari* (one day).

grammars.title: Hundreds, thousands, millions
body: Above a hundred, nothing new happens — you keep stacking the same pieces.
after: ⚠️ **The decimal point and comma are swapped compared with English.** Indonesian writes *Rp15.000* for fifteen thousand and *1,5 kg* for one and a half kilos. Misreading a price tag by a factor of a thousand is a rite of passage; do it in a shop, not at a property agent.

💬 **The thousands are often simply dropped in speech.** A seller may say *dua puluh lima* ("twenty-five") and mean 25,000 — everybody knows the mangoes are not twenty-five rupiah. You will also hear *seceng* (1,000) and *goceng* (5,000) in Jakarta, and *rebu* instead of *ribu* almost everywhere.

sections.title: Counting things, and the word orang

blocks.text: Indonesian likes a small word between the number and the noun — a classifier, of the kind Chinese and Thai also use. At A1 you can survive on three, and honestly you can survive on one.

The last row is not a shortcut this book invented: leaving the classifier out is entirely normal in conversation. What you must not do is get *orang* wrong — using *ekor* (the animal classifier, literally "tail") for a person is a real insult, not a cute mistake.

Measures behave the same way and are far more useful day to day: *sekilo* (a kilo), *setengah kilo* (half a kilo), *seporsi* (a portion), *segelas* (a glass), *sebotol* (a bottle), *sebungkus* (a packet).

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Bargain only where bargaining belongs.** Traditional markets, street stalls, souvenir shops, becak and unmetered transport: yes, and cheerfully. Restaurants, supermarkets, pharmacies, anywhere with a till: no. Pushing hard for a few thousand rupiah in the wrong place reads as mean rather than clever.
